To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
reporting eGFR in hospitalized patients did not improve the management of patients with mild renal dysfunction.
reporting eGFR in hospitalized patients did not improve the management of renal disease.
the implementation of a policy requiring the reporting of estimated glomerular rate did not improve the management of hospitalized non-chronically kidney disease patients.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effect of reporting eGFr on the management of patients.
the impact of the reporting of estimated glomerular filtrate rate (eGFr) on the management of hospitalised patients.
the effect of eGFR reporting on patient care.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
reporting eGFR does not change the renal management in hospitalized patients.
reporting eGFR in the laboratory report of hospitalized patients does not change the prescription habits of nephrotoxic medication, the hydration for radiological contrast studies and the use of NAC.
reporting eGFR in patients who are already being followed by a nephrologist does not change the management of the patient.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
eGFR reporting did not improve renal management.
reporting eGFR is not a cost-effective intervention.
reporting eGFR is not a cost-effective measure to improve the renal management in hospitalized patients.

the reporting of eGFR did have a significant impact in the clinical practice, and the impact was not as expected.
the impact of reporting estimated GFR is not as great as we had hoped.
eGFR does not improve patient care in the acute setting.
